title: Executive Summary
text: This document defines the business requirements for Nomni Procure , the rebuilt, AI-native successor to Zeemart. It supersedes the previous "HQ Module Enhancements" BRD and broadens scope from incremental HQ enhancements to a full product repositioning. The strategic intent is to move Nomni Procure from a procurement tool to the operating system for multi-outlet F&B procurement — combining centralised HQ governance, a full procure-to-pay lifecycle, real-time cost intelligence, and a named-agent AI layer that executes work rather than merely reporting on it. The rebuild follows a Strangler Fig approach: the existing Java/MongoDB backend is preserved behind a headless API layer, while the frontend, analytics, and agentic capabilities are built new. Two competitors anchor the competitive analysis: Restoke (AI-led restaurant management, strongest in automated insights and invoice intelligence) and Supy (multi-branch inventory and procurement control, strongest in approval workflows, central kitchen operations, and granular permissions). A structured review of the current platform knowledge base (§4) establishes the baseline: ordering, approvals, GRN receiving, 2/3-way match, invoice digitisation, PEPPOL e-invoicing, and a live supplier product (Nomni Supply) already exist — while HQ governance, agentic AI, unified variance analytics, and the marketplace layer are the genuine gaps. Nomni Procure must reach parity on competitor table-stakes and win on three differentiators: a transactional supplier network , agentic execution with human-grade guardrails , and HQ governance depth at 100+ outlet scale . Attribute Detail Document version 2.3 (supersedes BRD for HQ Module Enhancements v1.x) Status Draft for executive review Date June 2026 Product Nomni Procure (formerly Zeemart) Classification Internal · Confidential Geography Southeast Asia · Australia · Middle East & Africa

title: Background & Strategy
text: Zeemart established a position in Southeast Asia as a B2B procurement platform connecting F&B buyers with suppliers. The existing HQ Module BRD addressed governance pain for multi-outlet groups. Those requirements remain valid, but the market has moved: the category is consolidating around AI-powered back-of-house platforms, with global players (including Oracle NetSuite Restaurant Operations, launched March 2026) entering the space. At the same time, AI capability has changed what "good" looks like. Restoke markets itself as an AI restaurant manager whose agentic features handle ordering, prep, and task distribution. Supy positions as the data-driven operating system for multi-branch restaurants. A rebuilt Nomni Procure that simply modernises the UI would launch at parity with 2024; this BRD specifies a product that leads in 2026 and beyond. 2.1 Why now The frontend/UX of the current platform is dated and constrains adoption, particularly for outlet-level users on mobile. The architecture decision is made: headless API layer over the existing Java/MongoDB backend (Strangler Fig), enabling a new AI-native frontend without a backend rewrite. Competitors are converting our addressable market: both Restoke and Supy are active in Singapore and Australia, directly overlapping our core geography. AI-assisted delivery (Claude Code, parallel agent sessions) compresses the rebuild timeline to an estimated 5–6 months, making a leapfrog release commercially viable.

title: Competitive Analysis
text: This section summarises the two reference competitors and derives the capability bar Nomni Procure must meet or beat. Claims are drawn from public product material as of June 2026 and should be re-validated quarterly. 3.1 Restoke (restoke.ai) Positioning: "AI-powered restaurant management" — an AI restaurant manager that unifies POS, accounting, suppliers, and team operations. Founded 2020 in Melbourne; 2,000+ venues across AU, NZ, Singapore, the US, and the UK. Restaurant Intelligence: dashboard insights across purchases and sales, live COGS from POS integration, automatic trend and driver detection, multi-venue analytics with deeper HQ and CPK modules. Invoice intelligence: AI/OCR invoice scanning, automatic categorisation and reconciliation, one-click sync to accounting platforms. Agentic operations: AI used as a task manager for ordering, prep, and to-do lists distributed to staff devices; auto-ingests and maps purchasing, scheduling, and sales data on onboarding. Automated procurement: par-level driven ordering — scheduled orders checked against optimal stock levels; any vendor can be connected. Team management: checklists, training modules, task assignment. Claimed outcomes: 15.6% reduction in F&B costs; 10.1% labour cost reduction from automation. Assessment: Restoke's strength is breadth of automation and the "AI manager" narrative. Its HQ module is comparatively shallow on governance — it centralises visibility more than it enforces control. 3.2 Supy (supy.io) Positioning: "The operating system for multi-branch restaurants." 3,000+ restaurants in 30+ countries; strong in the Gulf and expanding globally. Full procurement lifecycle: requisitions → multi-level approvals → purchase orders → receiving → invoice reconciliation, on mobile or portal, with live price-variance monitoring and spend limits. title: Data Architecture
text: A foundational change to the Nomni Procure data model: the shift from supplier-primary (items exist only if a supplier lists them) to buyer-primary (buyers own a canonical item master; supplier SKUs are fulfillment options linked to it). 5.1 Current model constraints Buyers cannot create items for goods sourced outside the platform. Recipes and inventory can only reference items with an active supplier SKU. Switching supplier for an item breaks its linkage to recipes, inventory, and historical orders. Items produced in-house (central kitchen prep items, own-brand goods) cannot be represented at all. 5.2 Target model Internal Item — buyer-owned, exists independently of any supplier. Anchor for recipes, inventory, par levels, COGS, and reporting. Supplier SKU Link — connects an internal item to one or more supplier catalogue entries, each with its own price, pack size, UOM conversion, and lead time. Preferred Link — per-outlet or per-group designation of the default fulfillment source, with fallback alternatives. Internal item Supplier Supplier SKU Pack size Price White Sugar Supplier A WHT-SUGAR-25KG 25 kg bag $42.00 White Sugar Supplier B REF-SUGAR-1KG 1 kg bag $2.20 White Sugar Central Kitchen (internal) CK-SUGAR-OUT 5 kg transfer Cost price Recipes, inventory, par levels, and variance reports always reference the internal item . Ordering references the supplier SKU link . Changing supplier does not touch recipes or inventory history. 5.3 Operating modes Mode Who controls the item master Supplier SKU linking HQ Mode HQ Administrator creates and owns all internal items. Outlets read and consume; cannot create items. HQ links supplier SKUs. Outlets order via those links. HQ sets preferred supplier per group or outlet. Standalone Mode The outlet itself creates and owns its item master. No group governance layer. Outlet links its own suppliers' SKUs. Same one-to-many mechanic, controlled by the outlet. title: Ideal Customer Profiles
text: Three ICPs define the addressable market for Nomni Procure at launch. Every product decision — feature prioritisation, pricing, onboarding design, agent autonomy defaults, and support model — should be sanity-checked against these profiles. Geography: Southeast Asia, Australia, and Middle East & Africa. 6.1 ICP 1 — SMB Operator Attribute Profile Who they are Independent restaurant, cafe, bar, food truck, ghost kitchen, catering business, or small multi-concept operator. Owner or manager is typically the same person. 1–10 outlets, each often operating independently. Size signal 1–10 outlets. No dedicated procurement team — the owner, chef, or outlet manager handles ordering. Operating mode Standalone Mode. Each outlet controls its own item master, supplier links, and ordering. Current tools Spreadsheets, WhatsApp ordering, paper GRNs, or entry-level tools. Xero/MYOB for accounting. Primary pain Time lost on manual ordering and invoice chasing; no visibility of actual vs theoretical food cost; price changes caught late. What they buy Ordering, invoice digitisation, basic inventory and stock counts, spending reports, recipe costing, POS integration. What they don't need HQ governance, multi-level approvals, central kitchen workflows, RFQ, complex reporting. Price sensitivity High. Max ~$200/outlet/month. Must feel like it saves more than it costs within month one. Onboarding 100% self-serve. Signup, onboarding, supplier connection, and first order without any Nomni human intervention. Time-to-first-order target: same day. Markets Australia (independent cafes, bars), Singapore (cloud kitchens), UAE/KSA (independent dining). 6.2 ICP 2 — F&B Group (Mid-Market) Attribute Profile Who they are A growing F&B group with multiple outlets under one or more brands, with a Central Kitchen (CK) supplying some or all outlets. Outlets buy from both external suppliers and the CK. Size signal ~10–50 outlets. One or more brands. At least one Central Kitchen entity. May include franchise

title: Vision & Objectives
text: 7.1 Product vision Every multi-outlet F&B group runs procurement, inventory, recipes, and cost control through Nomni Procure — with HQ defining policy once, outlets executing within guardrails, suppliers transacting natively on the platform, and Nomni agents doing the repetitive work: drafting orders, reconciling invoices, flagging variances, and surfacing decisions that need a human. 7.2 Business objectives O1 — Category leadership: be the reference platform for multi-outlet procurement governance in SEA, AU, and MEA within 18 months of GA. O2 — Centralised governance: HQ defines and enforces market lists, recipes, inventory standards, and POS mappings with zero manual per-outlet effort. O3 — Effort reduction: reduce outlet-level time on ordering, receiving, and reconciliation by 50%+ through automation and agentic workflows. O4 — Cost intelligence: give HQ live COGS, stock variance, and spend analytics trusted enough to drive weekly decisions. O5 — Network effects: grow the transactional supplier network so switching away from Nomni Procure means losing supplier connectivity, not just software. O6 — Data accuracy & auditability: every HQ and agent action is logged, attributable, and reversible where applicable. 7.3 Non-goals (this release) NG1 — Workforce management: rostering, scheduling, and payroll are out of scope — integrate with Restoke/Tanda instead. NG2 — Front-of-house: no POS, reservations, or guest-facing capabilities. We integrate with POS, we do not replace it. NG3 — Accounting: no general ledger. Export and sync to accounting platforms. NG4 — Backend re-platform: the Java/MongoDB core is wrapped, not rewritten. NG5 — Fully autonomous purchasing: agents draft and recommend; humans approve above configured thresholds.

title: User Roles & Access
text: The original two-role model is retained and extended. The roles below are shipped templates over a permission engine, not hard-coded roles. Target: 200+ discrete permissions, composable and enforced at the API layer. Role Description Key permissions HQ Administrator Group-level owner of procurement governance. Full read/write on all group and outlet data; create/edit/push market lists, recipes, inventory, POS mappings; configure policies, thresholds, and agents. HQ Approver Finance or ops leader who approves sensitive changes and high-value orders. Approve/reject recipe changes, mapping overwrites, POs above threshold; read-only elsewhere. Outlet Manager Runs procurement at one or more outlets. Raise requisitions and orders within policy; manage par levels and outlet lists; receive goods; cannot modify HQ-pushed content. Outlet User Day-to-day staff (counting, receiving). Read HQ-defined data; stock counts; receiving confirmation; no edit/delete of HQ content. Finance User Reconciliation and export. Invoice review, 3-way match exceptions, exports to accounting; read-only operations data. Supplier User Trades on the network. Manage catalogue and pricing; receive POs; confirm or propose changes; issue e-invoices; no buyer data beyond own trades. Permissions are granular and composable (200+ discrete permissions), grouped into shipped role templates; groups can clone and customise. All permissions enforced at the API layer, not only in the UI. Outlet users see no edit controls on HQ-pushed content; locked records carry a visible 'Managed by HQ' state.

title: Functional Requirements
text: 10.1 Market List Assignment ML-1 — HQ can organise and manage market lists by outlet grouping (brand → region → state → outlet). ML-2 — HQ can assign a market list — or individual items — to all outlets in a group or a selected subset. ML-3 — Changes to an assigned market list propagate automatically to all assigned outlets, with per-outlet status (propagated / pending / error). ML-4 — Propagation never affects in-flight orders containing removed or modified items. ML-5 — Scheduled propagation: HQ can stage changes to take effect at a future date/time. ML-6 — Conflict surface: where an outlet-level exception exists, propagation flags rather than silently overwrites. ML-7 — Nomni agent can draft market-list updates from supplier price-file changes for HQ one-click approval. 10.2 Recipe Management RC-1 — HQ can create and maintain a central recipe library, including sub-recipes/prep recipes. RC-2 — Pushed recipes are locked for outlet users — ingredients and quantities cannot be modified. RC-3 — Full version history with timestamps and author; HQ can roll back to any prior version. RC-4 — Recipes include selling price, synced bidirectionally with POS price. RC-5 — Live recipe costing: ingredient cost changes recompute recipe cost and margin in real time. RC-6 — Margin alerts: configurable thresholds trigger notification when price changes push a recipe below target margin, with agent-suggested responses. RC-7 — Approval workflow: recipe changes can require HQ Approver sign-off before propagation. RC-8 — Allergen and nutrition fields per recipe, propagated with the recipe. 10.3 Inventory Management IN-1 — HQ defines a master inventory item list (name, category, UOM) and pushes it to outlets or outlet groups. IN-2 — Outlets can organise HQ-defined items into their own lists; items can appear in multiple lists. title: Experience & Design
text: UX-1 — All UI built on the Nomni Design System (v1.6+): documented tokens and component registry only; agent surfaces use the agent signature treatment (named agent, approve/undo states). UX-2 — Mobile-first for outlet workflows (requisitions, receiving, counts); desktop-optimised for HQ governance and analytics. UX-3 — Status is never conveyed by colour alone; WCAG AA contrast minimums enforced at build. UX-4 — Command menu (⌘K) for HQ power users: jump to any outlet, recipe, item, or report. UX-5 — Onboarding auto-ingests existing data (item lists, supplier files, POS exports) with AI-assisted mapping. Time-to-first-value under one day for a new group. UX-6 — Multi-language support: English at GA; Bahasa, Thai, Vietnamese, and Simplified Chinese on the roadmap.

title: Non-Functional Requirements
text: 12.1 Architecture NF-1 — Headless, API-first: all functionality exposed through a documented API layer wrapping the existing Java/MongoDB backend. New frontend is exclusively an API consumer. NF-2 — Public API and webhooks for customer and partner integrations. NF-3 — AI layer consumes the same governed APIs; agent context is permission-scoped. 12.2 Performance & scale NF-4 — Support 100+ outlets per group and 500+ concurrent users without degradation; dashboard queries return in under 3 seconds at p95. NF-5 — Propagation operations complete across 100+ outlets within 60 seconds with per-outlet status. 12.3 Security & access control NF-6 — Role-based access enforced at the API layer; granular permission engine per §8. NF-7 — Approval workflows for sensitive changes (recipes, mappings, high-value POs). NF-8 — SSO (SAML/OIDC) for enterprise groups; MFA available for all roles. NF-9 — Data isolation per tenant; supplier users cannot access buyer data beyond own trades. 12.4 Auditability NF-10 — Full audit logs for all HQ actions and agent actions — searchable and exportable. NF-11 — Agent actions carry rationale summaries sufficient for a human reviewer to understand why the action was taken. 12.5 Reliability & data NF-12 — 99.9% availability target for ordering and receiving paths. NF-13 — Offline-tolerant mobile flows for stock counts and receiving (queue and sync). NF-14 — Data residency options for SG/AU enterprise customers.

title: Delivery & Phasing
text: Six-phase Strangler Fig programme (~5–6 months with AI-assisted development). The Marketlist MVP ships to production in Phase 4 as proof of concept — the explicit mitigation for the stall risk observed in comparable modernisation programmes. Phase Content Duration 1 Backend audit & API readiness (Java/MongoDB review, API contract draft) 2–3 weeks 2 API wrapper & headless layer; contracts locked 4–6 weeks (parallel with 3) 3 UI/UX design system application & screen design (Claude-assisted) 4–5 weeks (parallel with 2) 4 Marketlist MVP live (incl. first agent surface: governance agent drafts) 4–6 weeks 5 Recipes, Inventory, POS Mapping, Procure-to-Pay, Invoice Intelligence, Analytics 6–8 weeks 6 Integration, performance at 100+ outlet scale, security review, hardening 3–4 weeks Fast follow Central Kitchen module; Supplier Network marketplace expansion; additional agents Post-GA roadmap Key risk to manage: research across 41 similar Strangler Fig projects shows 68% stall before 90 days. The mitigation: ship the Marketlist MVP to production in Phase 4. A live product in users' hands creates accountability and validates the architecture before committing full resources to the rollout.

title: Open Questions
text: OQ-1 (Engineering, blocking): Phase 1 audit outcome — which backend endpoints are exposable as-is vs requiring adapters? OQ-2 (Product): Default agent autonomy thresholds per region/segment — what order value requires approval out of the box? OQ-3 (Commercial): Pricing model — per outlet per month (Supy-style) vs platform fee + network take rate; marketplace monetisation. OQ-4 (Data/Legal): Anonymised price benchmarking (SN-4) — consent model and competition-law review per market. OQ-5 (Product): POS integration priority order beyond Abacus for AU/SEA coverage. OQ-6 (Engineering): PEPPOL e-invoicing exists today for SG — what is required to extend coverage to AU eInvoicing and other markets through the new API layer?

title: Conclusion
text: This BRD carries forward every commitment of the original HQ Module Enhancements document and extends it to a product that can lead its category. The competitive analysis is direct about the bar: Supy defines operational rigour, Restoke defines AI ambition. Nomni Procure's winning position combines both and adds what neither has — a transactional supplier network and an agent layer with enterprise-grade governance, delivered on an API-first architecture that compounds. Three foundational decisions differentiate this release: the buyer-primary data model (§5) flips the power structure from supplier-led to buyer-led; the three ICP model (§6) ensures the product serves SMB self-serve, mid-market hybrid, and enterprise governance without conflating them; and the agent layer with hard guardrails (§10.8) makes AI a trusted execution partner rather than an experimental feature. Approval of this document authorises Phase 1 (backend audit) to proceed immediately.
